s.u1.title: Moving compared to what
s.u1.blurb: Nothing is moving or still on its own account. It is moving compared to something, and that something has to be named first.
s.u2.title: Steady, or not steady
s.u2.blurb: Equal distances in equal times, or not. And the one number that says how fast.
s.u3.title: Speed that remembers the way
s.u3.blurb: Velocity is speed with a direction attached. The difference shows up the moment you turn round.
s.u4.title: Velocity that will not sit still
s.u4.blurb: Acceleration is not a word for going fast. It says how quickly the velocity is changing.
s.u5.title: The same journey, drawn twice
s.u5.blurb: Distance against time, and velocity against time. Four things live on those two pictures.
s.u6.title: Three equations
s.u6.blurb: When the acceleration is steady, three short equations answer almost any question you can ask.
s.u7.title: Round and round
s.u7.blurb: A steady speed around a circle is accelerated motion. That one sentence is the whole topic.
ch7.u1.reference:
Sit in a moving bus and the trees outside slide backwards. Stand on the road and the trees do not move at all: the bus does. Neither of you is wrong. Motion is always measured against something else, and that something has to be picked before any answer means anything.

The thing you measure from is the reference point, also called the origin. Say the school is 2 km north of the railway station and you have located the school, because you named the station. Drop the station and the 2 km says nothing at all.

Choose the origin to suit yourself. There is no correct one, only a convenient one.
a.ch7-u1-read-1.title: Moving compared to what?
ch7.u1.corners.predict.prompt: You go from one corner of the playground to the opposite corner, but along the two edges instead of cutting across. Compare how far you walked with how far you ended up from the start.
ch7.u1.corners.predict.o0: They come to the same number
ch7.u1.corners.predict.o1: The walk is the longer of the two
ch7.u1.corners.predict.o2: The walk is the shorter of the two
ch7.u1.corners.predict.o3: It depends on how fast you walk
ch7.u1.corners.observe: Lay the rope corner to corner and compare it with what the tape read along the two edges.
ch7.u1.corners.explain: Walking the edges adds both edges together. The rope across the middle is the straight line between start and finish, and a straight line is the shortest route between two points, so it can never be the longer of the two.
ch7.u1.do.steps:
1. Mark two opposite corners of a rectangular court or playground with chalk. Call them A and C.
2. Walk from A along one edge to the next corner, then along the second edge to C. Measure each edge as you go and write both numbers down.
3. Add the two edges. That total is the distance you covered.
4. Now stretch the rope straight from A to C and measure it. That is the magnitude of your displacement.
5. Write the two numbers side by side. Repeat for a different pair of corners.
ch7.u1.do.watch: A group that walks the two edges and then reports the rope length as the distance. Ask them which number their legs would agree with.
a.ch7-u1-do-2.title: Two corners of the ground
a.ch7-u1-do-2.blurb: Walk the two edges of the playground, then measure straight across. Two numbers for one journey.
ch7.u1.sort.i0.label: What the odometer of an autorickshaw shows at the end of the day
ch7.u1.sort.i0.why: It counts wheel turns, so every metre driven goes on, including the way back.
ch7.u1.sort.i1.label: How far you are from home when the trip is over
ch7.u1.sort.i1.why: Only the two ends matter: where you began and where you stopped.
ch7.u1.sort.i2.label: Can come out as zero even after a very long journey
ch7.u1.sort.i2.why: A round trip finishes where it started, so the straight line between the ends has no length.
ch7.u1.sort.i3.label: Is never the smaller of the two
ch7.u1.sort.i3.why: The straight line is the shortest route between two points, so the route actually taken is at least as long.
ch7.u1.sort.i4.label: Is not fully stated until a direction is given
ch7.u1.sort.i4.why: 35 km is not an answer. 35 km east is.
ch7.u1.sort.i5.label: Keeps growing when you turn round and come back
ch7.u1.sort.i5.why: Nothing you do afterwards can take a metre off it.
ask.ch7-u1-sort-3.bigger.q: Can the displacement ever be bigger than the distance?
ask.ch7-u1-sort-3.bigger.a:
No, not once. The displacement is the straight line between where you started and where you finished, and no route between two points is shorter than the straight line between them.

They can be equal, and that is worth knowing too. It happens when the motion is along a straight line and never turns back. For that one case, and only that one, the two numbers agree.
a.ch7-u1-sort-3.title: Distance or displacement?
a.ch7-u1-sort-3.blurb: Each statement is true of exactly one of the two. Deciding which is most of this topic.
ch7.u1.calc.c0.prompt: A cyclist rides 40 m east along a straight road, then turns and rides 15 m back west. What distance has she covered?
ch7.u1.calc.c0.s0: Distance adds every stretch, whichever way it points
ch7.u1.calc.c0.trap: Subtracting to get 25. That is the displacement, not the distance.
ch7.u1.calc.c1.prompt: The same ride. How far is she from where she started?
ch7.u1.calc.c1.g0: 40 m east, then 15 m back west
ch7.u1.calc.c1.s0: Displacement counts start and finish only
ch7.u1.calc.c1.s1: She ends up 40 minus 15 east of the start
ch7.u1.calc.c1.trap: Adding to get 55. That is how far she pedalled, not how far she got.
ch7.u1.calc.c2.prompt: She now rides the last 25 m back to her starting point. What is her displacement for the whole ride?
ch7.u1.calc.c2.g0: She finishes exactly where she began
ch7.u1.calc.c2.s0: Start and finish are the same point
ch7.u1.calc.c2.s1: The straight line between a point and itself has no length
ch7.u1.calc.c2.trap: Answering 80, which is the total distance. Displacement forgets the route completely.
a.ch7-u1-calc-4.title: One road, three answers
ch7.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: A runner finishes one full lap of a 400 m track. What is her displacement?
ch7.u1.quiz.q0.f0: That is the distance she covered. Her displacement is a different question.
ch7.u1.quiz.q0.f1: Right. She finishes at the point she started from, so the straight line between them has no length.
ch7.u1.quiz.q0.f2: Half a lap would put her across the track. A full lap brings her home.
ch7.u1.quiz.q0.f3: It can, and it is zero. Nothing about a lap is unknown.
ch7.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: Can the distance covered be smaller than the magnitude of the displacement?
ch7.u1.quiz.q1.o0: Yes, if the object moves fast enough
ch7.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Speed has nothing to do with it.
ch7.u1.quiz.q1.f1: A curved path makes the distance larger, not smaller.
ch7.u1.quiz.q1.f2: Right. The displacement is the shortest route between the two ends, so nothing can be shorter than it.
ch7.u1.quiz.q1.f3: A circle is the clearest case of the opposite: a long distance and a small displacement.
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.prompt: Why is 35 km not a complete statement of a displacement?
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.o0: Because a displacement must also say which way
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.f0: Right. A size on its own leaves you standing somewhere on a circle of possible finishing points.
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.o1: Because displacement is always larger than that
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.f1: Size is not the problem here. The missing direction is.
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.o2: Because the distance covered has to be given alongside it
ch7.u1.quiz.q2.f2: They answer different questions, and each one stands on its own.
a.ch7-u1-quiz-5.title: Distance and displacement
ch7.u2.sort.i0.label: A train covering 10 km in each of five successive minutes
ch7.u2.sort.i0.why: Same distance, same time, every time. That is the definition and nothing more is needed.
ch7.u2.sort.i1.label: A bus on a crowded market road
ch7.u2.sort.i1.why: It crawls, stops, picks up again. The distance per minute changes constantly.
ch7.u2.sort.i2.label: Readings of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 m taken a minute apart
ch7.u2.sort.i2.why: The gaps are 10, 10, 10 and 10. Equal distances in equal times.
ch7.u2.sort.i3.label: Readings of 12, 19, 23, 35 and 37 m taken a minute apart
ch7.u2.sort.i3.why: The gaps are 7, 4, 12 and 2. Nothing equal about them.
ch7.u2.sort.i4.label: A stone dropped from a roof
ch7.u2.sort.i4.why: It falls further in each second than in the one before, right up to the ground.
ch7.u2.sort.i5.label: A ball rolling across a level floor and gradually slowing
ch7.u2.sort.i5.why: Slowing down is a change of speed, so the distance per second keeps shrinking.
a.ch7-u2-sort-1.title: Equal distances in equal times?
a.ch7-u2-sort-1.blurb: One test, applied six times. Does it cover the same ground in every equal stretch of time?
ch7.u2.lab.predict.prompt: The trolley is already moving at 5 metres per second and nothing is pushing it. There is no friction. What will the distance-time graph look like over the next six seconds?
ch7.u2.lab.observe: Run the first task and watch the distance-time graph as it draws itself.
ch7.u2.lab.explain: Equal distances in equal times draw a straight line. The line is straight exactly because the speed never changes, and that is what uniform motion means. Nothing in the picture is about how fast: a slower trolley would draw a straight line too, just a gentler one.
ch7.u2.lab.t1.label: Leave the push at zero and run it.
ch7.u2.lab.t1.asks: Is the distance-time line straight or curved? Say what that tells you about the speed.
ch7.u2.lab.t2.label: Now set the push to 3 newtons.
ch7.u2.lab.t2.asks: The distance-time line bends. Are equal distances still being covered in equal times?
ch7.u2.lab.t3.label: Push as hard as the slider will go.
ch7.u2.lab.t3.asks: One of the two graphs is still a straight line. Which one, and why is it the one that stays straight?
ch7.u2.lab.closing: A straight distance-time line is the signature of uniform motion. The moment it bends, the speed is changing.
ask.ch7-u2-lab-2.friction.q: A real trolley slows down and stops. Why does this one not?
ask.ch7-u2-lab-2.friction.a:
Because friction has been set to zero, which is a choice made for this lab and not a fact about trolleys.

It is worth doing. A real trolley slowing down tells you two things at once, the motion and the rubbing, and you cannot see either clearly. Switch the rubbing off and what is left is the plain statement that something already moving, with nothing acting on it, simply carries on.

That statement turns out to be a law, and chapter 8 is where it gets its name.
a.ch7-u2-lab-2.title: A trolley with nothing pushing it
a.ch7-u2-lab-2.blurb: Friction is switched off here, so the trolley does what the textbook's object does: exactly what it was already doing.
ch7.u2.speed:
Speed is distance divided by time. Its SI unit is the metre per second, written m/s, and you will also meet km/h for vehicles and cm/s for small slow things.

Almost nothing holds one speed for a whole journey, so the number people quote is the average speed: the whole distance divided by the whole time. A car that averages 50 km/h over two hours is not promising a single moment at 50. It is promising 100 km.

Averages hide things, and that is the point of them. The hiding is only a problem when someone forgets it is happening.
a.ch7-u2-read-3.title: Average speed, and why it is an average
ch7.u2.calc.c0.prompt: A boy walks 150 m in 50 s, then runs the next 150 m in 25 s. What is his average speed?
ch7.u2.calc.c0.trap: Averaging 3 m/s and 6 m/s to get 4.5. That is right only when equal times are spent at each speed, and here they are not.
ch7.u2.calc.c1.prompt: A car's odometer reads 14,200 km at the start of a trip and 14,580 km at the end. The trip took 8 hours. What was the average speed?
ch7.u2.calc.c1.s0: The distance is the difference, not the final reading
ch7.u2.calc.c1.trap: Dividing 14,580 by 8. The odometer has been counting since the day the car was built.
ch7.u2.calc.c2.prompt: A milk van drives out to a village at an average 20 km/h and comes back along the same road at 30 km/h. What is its average speed for the round trip?
ch7.u2.calc.c2.g0: Same road each way, so the same distance each way
ch7.u2.calc.c2.g1: Out at 20 km/h, back at 30 km/h
ch7.u2.calc.c2.s0: Call the one-way distance d. Going takes d over 20, returning takes d over 30
ch7.u2.calc.c2.s1: Total time is d over 20 plus d over 30, which comes to d over 12
ch7.u2.calc.c2.s3: Divide 2d by d over 12, and the d cancels
ch7.u2.calc.c2.trap: Averaging 20 and 30 to get 25. More of the trip's time is spent at the slower speed, so the true average is pulled below the middle.
a.ch7-u2-calc-4.title: Working out an average
ch7.u2.quiz.q0.prompt: Equal distances covered in equal intervals of time. What is that motion called?
ch7.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and notice that the definition says nothing at all about being fast.
ch7.u2.quiz.q0.f1: Accelerated motion is the opposite: unequal distances in equal times.
ch7.u2.quiz.q0.f2: A circular path is about shape. Uniform is about equal distances in equal times, and the path can be dead straight.
ch7.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: A bus covers 60 km in the first hour and 40 km in the next two hours. What is its average speed?
ch7.u2.quiz.q1.f1: That is the average of 60 and 40, and it ignores that the second stretch took twice as long.
ch7.u2.quiz.q1.f2: That is the speed over the second stretch alone.
ch7.u2.quiz.q1.f3: That is 40 km over 2 hours, which is only half the journey.
ch7.u2.quiz.q2.prompt: What does the odometer of a vehicle measure?
ch7.u2.quiz.q2.f0: Right. It counts wheel turns, so it adds up every metre.
ch7.u2.quiz.q2.o1: How far it is from where it started
ch7.u2.quiz.q2.f1: That would be the displacement, and no odometer knows it.
ch7.u2.quiz.q2.f2: That is the speedometer, the other dial.
ch7.u2.quiz.q2.o3: The time it has been running
a.ch7-u2-quiz-5.title: Speed and uniform motion
ch7.u3.velocity:
Speed says how fast. Velocity says how fast and which way. Both are measured in metres per second, and on a journey in one straight line that never turns back they come to the same number.

A velocity changes if the speed changes, or if the direction changes, or if both do. Hold on to that middle one. A car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h has a changing velocity the whole way round, even though its speedometer never moves.

When the velocity changes at a steady rate, the average velocity is easy to find: add the starting velocity to the finishing one and halve it. That shortcut is only allowed while the rate of change is steady.
a.ch7-u3-read-1.title: Velocity: speed that remembers the way
ch7.u3.calc.c0.prompt: A swimmer swims the length of a 50 m pool and back, four lengths in all, in 100 s. What is her average speed?
ch7.u3.calc.c0.s0: Average speed uses the whole distance: 4 times 50
ch7.u3.calc.c0.trap: Using 50 m as the distance. Every length counts towards the distance.
ch7.u3.calc.c1.prompt: The same swim. What is her average velocity?
ch7.u3.calc.c1.g0: She finishes at the end of the pool she started from
ch7.u3.calc.c1.s0: Average velocity uses displacement, not distance
ch7.u3.calc.c1.s1: Start and finish are the same point, so the displacement is zero
ch7.u3.calc.c1.trap: Answering 2 m/s again. Average speed and average velocity ask different questions about the same swim.
ch7.u3.calc.c2.prompt: A train speeds up smoothly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s along a straight track. What is its average velocity over that stretch?
ch7.u3.calc.c2.g2: The velocity changes at a steady rate
ch7.u3.calc.c2.s0: When the change is steady, the average is the mean of the two ends
ch7.u3.calc.c2.trap: Reaching for this shortcut on a journey where the velocity changes unevenly. On a train in traffic it gives the wrong answer.
ask.ch7-u3-calc-2.zerovelocity.q: If the average velocity is zero, does that mean nothing happened?
ask.ch7-u3-calc-2.zerovelocity.a:
Not at all. It means the finish was the start.

Average velocity is a statement about the two ends of a journey and it is completely silent about everything in between. The swimmer covered 200 m, got tired and used up her hundred seconds, and none of that shows.

This is why a report of a journey almost always gives the average speed instead. Average velocity is the right quantity when direction is the point, as it is in navigation, and a poor one when effort is the point.
a.ch7-u3-calc-2.title: There and back
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: When is the magnitude of the average velocity equal to the average speed?
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.o0: When the motion is along a straight line and never turns back
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Only then does the route have the same length as the straight line between the ends.
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.o1: When the object is moving quickly
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.f1: Speed has nothing to do with whether the two agree.
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.o2: When the object returns to its starting point
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.f2: That is the case where they differ most: the speed is large and the velocity is zero.
ch7.u3.quiz.q0.f3: They part company the moment the path stops being a straight line in one direction.
ch7.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: A car goes once round a circular track at a steady 40 km/h and stops where it started. Its average velocity for the lap is:
ch7.u3.quiz.q1.f0: That is its average speed. Average velocity asks about the displacement instead.
ch7.u3.quiz.q1.f1: Right. The displacement for a full lap is zero, so the average velocity is zero.
ch7.u3.quiz.q1.o2: 40 km/h, in the direction it set off
ch7.u3.quiz.q1.f2: A displacement of zero has no direction to carry, so nothing is left pointing anywhere.
ch7.u3.quiz.q1.f3: It can, and it is zero. The lap hands you both ends of the journey and they are the same point.
ch7.u3.quiz.q2.prompt: Which of these can change while the speed stays exactly the same?
ch7.u3.quiz.q2.o0: The velocity, if the direction changes
ch7.u3.quiz.q2.f0: Right, and this is the single most useful sentence in the chapter.
ch7.u3.quiz.q2.o1: The distance from the start, which holds steady too
ch7.u3.quiz.q2.f1: A steady speed means the distance grows steadily. It stops growing only when the speed is zero.
ch7.u3.quiz.q2.f2: The velocity can, and it does so on every bend.
a.ch7-u3-quiz-3.title: Speed against velocity
ch7.u4.lab.predict.prompt: The trolley starts from rest and you give it a steady push that never lets up. What will the velocity-time graph look like?
ch7.u4.lab.observe: Run the first task and keep your eye on the velocity-time graph.
ch7.u4.lab.explain:
A steady push changes the velocity by the same amount in every second, and equal changes in equal times draw a straight sloping line. That is what uniform acceleration means.

Now look at the distance-time graph for the same run. It curves, because each second carries the trolley further than the second before it. One motion, two very different pictures.
ch7.u4.lab.t1.label: Push with 2 newtons and watch the velocity-time line.
ch7.u4.lab.t1.asks: By how much does the velocity rise in each second? Is it the same amount every second?
ch7.u4.lab.t2.label: Now push with 8 newtons.
ch7.u4.lab.t2.asks: The line is steeper. Which quantity does the steepness of a velocity-time line stand for?
ch7.u4.lab.t3.label: Keep the push at 8 and make the trolley five times heavier.
ch7.u4.lab.t3.asks: Same push, gentler slope. Say what has happened to the acceleration, and what has not changed.
ch7.u4.lab.closing: The slope of the velocity-time line is the acceleration. Nothing else on either graph gives it to you directly.
ask.ch7-u4-lab-1.heavier.q: Why does the same push give a smaller acceleration to a heavier trolley?
ask.ch7-u4-lab-1.heavier.a:
Because the acceleration depends on the mass as well as on the push, and the rule is a = F/m.

This chapter only measures acceleration. It asks how fast the velocity is changing and never asks why. The lab lets you move the mass slider because the effect is real and you will see it, but the explanation is not here.

Chapter 8 is where the push gets explained, and that one short equation is the whole of it.
a.ch7-u4-lab-1.title: What a steady push does to the graphs
a.ch7-u4-lab-1.blurb: Three runs. Watch the velocity-time line, and then notice what the other graph is doing at the same moment.
ch7.u4.calc.c0.prompt: A cyclist starting from rest reaches 6 m/s in 30 s. Find the acceleration.
ch7.u4.calc.c0.s0: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time
ch7.u4.calc.c0.trap: Dividing 30 by 6. Acceleration is velocity gained per second, not seconds per unit of velocity.
ch7.u4.calc.c1.prompt: The same cyclist then brakes from 6 m/s down to 4 m/s in 5 s. Find the acceleration.
ch7.u4.calc.c1.s0: Use the same rule, and keep the order: final minus initial
ch7.u4.calc.c1.trap: Dropping the minus sign. The sign is the information: it says the acceleration points against the motion.
ch7.u4.calc.c2.prompt: A train starting from rest reaches 54 km/h in 50 s. Find its acceleration in m/s².
ch7.u4.calc.c2.s0: The answer is wanted in m/s², so convert first
ch7.u4.calc.c2.s1: 54 km/h is 54 times 1000 over 3600, which is 15 m/s
ch7.u4.calc.c2.trap: Dividing 54 by 50 and leaving the units as they came. Mixing km/h with seconds gives a number that means nothing.
a.ch7-u4-calc-2.title: How fast the velocity is changing
ch7.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: A car is moving forwards and its acceleration is minus 2 m/s². What is happening?
ch7.u4.quiz.q0.f0: Right. The minus sign says the acceleration points against the motion.
ch7.u4.quiz.q0.f1: The car is still going forwards. It is the acceleration that points the other way.
ch7.u4.quiz.q0.f2: It is still moving. It will stop only when the velocity reaches zero.
ch7.u4.quiz.q0.f3: Then the acceleration would have the same sign as the velocity.
ch7.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: A ball thrown straight up is momentarily at rest at the top of its flight. What is its acceleration at that instant?
ch7.u4.quiz.q1.o0: Zero, because it is not moving
ch7.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Velocity and acceleration are different quantities. One of them being zero says nothing about the other.
ch7.u4.quiz.q1.f1: Right. Gravity does not pause while the ball turns round, which is exactly why it turns round.
ch7.u4.quiz.q1.o2: Upwards, which is what carried it up there
ch7.u4.quiz.q1.f2: Nothing pushes it up once it has left the hand. It rises because it was given speed, and gravity has been pulling it down throughout.
ch7.u4.quiz.q2.o0: The velocity rises by equal amounts in equal intervals of time
ch7.u4.quiz.q2.f0: Right, and a freely falling body is the standard example.
ch7.u4.quiz.q2.f1: That is uniform velocity, which means no acceleration at all.
ch7.u4.quiz.q2.o2: The object is moving in a circle
ch7.u4.quiz.q2.f2: Circular motion at a steady speed is accelerated, but the acceleration is not uniform in this sense.
ch7.u4.quiz.q2.f3: Acceleration is about change, not about how fast something is going.
a.ch7-u4-quiz-3.title: Acceleration
ch7.u5.lab.predict.prompt: An object is standing still. What does its distance-time graph look like?
ch7.u5.lab.observe: Run the first task and look at the distance-time graph.
ch7.u5.lab.explain: Its distance from the start is not changing, so the line holds the same height all the way across. Height on a distance-time graph tells you where the object is. It says nothing directly about how fast it is going: that is the slope.
ch7.u5.lab.t1.label: Leave the push at zero. The trolley is at rest.
ch7.u5.lab.t1.asks: Both lines are flat. Which of the two tells you the object is not moving, and how do you read it?
ch7.u5.lab.t2.label: No push, but start it off at 4 m/s.
ch7.u5.lab.t2.asks: A sloping straight line and a flat line. Say in one sentence what journey this pair describes.
ch7.u5.lab.t3.label: Start from rest and push steadily.
ch7.u5.lab.t3.asks: One line curves and one stays straight. Which is which, and what does the straight one's slope stand for?
ch7.u5.lab.closing: Four things live on these two graphs. Height on the distance-time graph is where it is. Slope of that graph is how fast. Height on the velocity-time graph is how fast. Slope of that one is the acceleration, and the area under it is the distance covered.
a.ch7-u5-lab-1.title: Three journeys, six graphs
a.ch7-u5-lab-1.blurb: The same two graphs, three times over. The job is to read them, not to run them.
ch7.u5.draw.caption: A velocity-time graph for steady speed. The shaded rectangle is the distance covered between the two times.
ch7.u5.draw.axes.label: The two axes
ch7.u5.draw.axes.do: Rule a vertical line up the left of the page and a horizontal one along the bottom, meeting at a corner. Time goes along the bottom, velocity up the side. Mark a scale on each.
ch7.u5.draw.axes.does: The corner where they meet is time zero and velocity zero. Every height on this graph is read from the bottom axis upwards.
ch7.u5.draw.line.label: The velocity line
ch7.u5.draw.line.do: The bus holds 40 km/h the whole time, so find 40 on the velocity axis and rule a line straight across the page at that height, parallel to the time axis.
ch7.u5.draw.line.does: A flat line on a velocity-time graph means the velocity is not changing. On a distance-time graph a flat line meant something completely different: stopped. The shape is the same and the meaning is not.
ch7.u5.draw.interval.label: The stretch of time you care about
ch7.u5.draw.interval.do: Pick two times on the bottom axis and call them t1 and t2. From each, rule a line straight up until it meets the velocity line.
ch7.u5.draw.interval.does: These two uprights fence off the part of the journey being asked about. Without them the graph describes the whole run and no particular stretch of it.
ch7.u5.draw.area.label: The area, which is the distance
ch7.u5.draw.area.do: Shade the rectangle you have just enclosed: the velocity line on top, the time axis below, the two uprights at the sides.
ch7.u5.draw.area.does: Its height is the velocity and its width is the time, so its area is velocity times time, which is the distance covered. The distance was never a number you had to be given. It was the space under the line all along.
ch7.u5.draw.area.p0: Area works for any velocity-time graph, not only a flat one.
ch7.u5.draw.area.p1: If the line slopes up from the origin, the shape underneath is a triangle, and its area is half the base times the height.
ch7.u5.draw.area.p2: If the line slopes up from some starting velocity, the shape is a rectangle with a triangle sitting on it. Work out both and add them.
ch7.u5.draw.area.p3: That sum is exactly s = ut + half a t squared, arrived at by cutting up a picture instead of by algebra.
ch7.u5.draw.area.p4: Nothing like this works on a distance-time graph. Area under that one means nothing at all.
ask.ch7-u5-draw-2.sloping.q: If the velocity line slopes instead of lying flat, does the area still give the distance?
ask.ch7-u5-draw-2.sloping.a:
Yes, every time. The rule is the area, not the rectangle.

A line sloping up from the origin leaves a triangle underneath, and a triangle's area is half the base times the height. A line sloping up from some starting velocity leaves a rectangle with a triangle sitting on top of it, so work out both and add them.

Do that addition in symbols and what comes out is s = ut + half a t squared, which is the second equation of motion. It is not a new fact. It is this picture, written down.
a.ch7-u5-draw-2.title: Draw the graph, then find the distance inside it
a.ch7-u5-draw-2.blurb: A bus holding a steady 40 km/h. Build the graph a line at a time, and the distance turns out to be sitting underneath it.
ch7.u5.sort.i0.label: A distance-time line that is flat
ch7.u5.sort.i0.why: Its distance from the start is not changing, so it is not going anywhere.
ch7.u5.sort.i1.label: A distance-time line that is straight and sloping
ch7.u5.sort.i1.why: Equal distances in equal times, which is uniform motion.
ch7.u5.sort.i2.label: A distance-time line that curves upward and keeps getting steeper
ch7.u5.sort.i2.why: Each second covers more ground than the one before it.
ch7.u5.sort.i3.label: A velocity-time line that is flat, above zero
ch7.u5.sort.i3.why: Flat means the velocity is not changing. On a distance-time graph flat meant stopped. Same shape, different graph, different meaning.
ch7.u5.sort.i4.label: A velocity-time line that is flat, along zero
ch7.u5.sort.i4.why: The velocity is zero and stays zero.
ch7.u5.sort.i5.label: A velocity-time line that is straight and sloping upward
ch7.u5.sort.i5.why: Equal gains in velocity in equal times, which is uniform acceleration.
a.ch7-u5-sort-3.title: What the shape is telling you
a.ch7-u5-sort-3.blurb: Six line shapes. The same shape can mean two different things, depending on which graph it is drawn on.
ch7.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: What does the area under a velocity-time graph give you?
ch7.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Height times width is velocity times time.
ch7.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Acceleration is the slope of that graph, not the area.
ch7.u5.quiz.q0.f2: That is a height on the graph, read at one instant.
ch7.u5.quiz.q0.f3: That is a width along the bottom axis.
ch7.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: Two straight lines on one distance-time graph, and one is steeper. What does the steeper one mean?
ch7.u5.quiz.q1.f0: Right. Slope on a distance-time graph is speed.
ch7.u5.quiz.q1.f1: Which has gone further is read off the height at whatever time you care about, and the gentler line can be higher.
ch7.u5.quiz.q1.f2: Where a line starts is a matter of where it meets the axis, not how steep it is.
ch7.u5.quiz.q1.f3: A straight line means no acceleration at all. A curve would mean acceleration.
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.prompt: A distance-time graph comes out as a straight sloping line, but the road the car took bends sharply. Is the graph wrong?
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.o0: Yes, the bend should show in the line
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.f0: Nothing on either axis is a direction, so a bend has nowhere to appear.
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.o1: No. The graph plots distance against time, not the shape of the road
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.f1: Right. It is a graph, not a map.
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.o2: Yes, a bent road always gives a curved graph
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.f2: The shape of the line comes from how the distance grows, and that can be perfectly steady on a winding road.
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.o3: The graph cannot be drawn for a bent road
ch7.u5.quiz.q2.f3: It can, and it looks exactly like the graph for a straight road at the same speed.
a.ch7-u5-quiz-4.title: Reading the graphs
ch7.u6.equations:
When the acceleration is steady, three short equations tie five quantities together: the starting velocity u, the finishing velocity v, the acceleration a, the time t and the distance s.

v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²
2as = v² − u²

Look at what each one leaves out. The first has no s in it. The second has no v. The third has no t. That is the whole trick to choosing one: find the quantity the question neither gives you nor asks for, and reach for the equation that does not contain it.

All three are worth nothing unless the acceleration is uniform. A bus in city traffic breaks every one of them.
a.ch7-u6-read-1.title: Three equations, and when you are allowed them
ch7.u6.item.bus: A bus starts from rest and accelerates at 0.1 m/s² for 2 minutes. How fast is it then going?
ch7.u6.item.train: A train moving at 25 m/s brakes at 0.5 m/s² against its motion. How far does it go before it stops?
ch7.u6.item.trolley: A trolley starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 6 s. How far does it travel?
ch7.u6.item.car: A car at 8 m/s accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 4 s. What is its velocity at the end?
ch7.u6.item.stone: A stone is dropped and falls 20 m, gaining 10 m/s of speed every second. How fast is it moving when it lands?
ask.ch7-u6-tree-2.twoways.q: Some problems seem to fit two of the equations. Is one of them wrong?
ask.ch7-u6-tree-2.twoways.a:
No. When a question gives you four of the five quantities there is often more than one honest route, and both get the same answer.

The tree picks the shortest one: the equation with no unknown in it but the one you want. Take any other route and you end up working out a quantity you were not asked for, and then using it. That is more arithmetic and more places to slip.

If two routes give you different answers, the mistake is in the arithmetic and not in the choice.
a.ch7-u6-tree-2.title: Which equation?
a.ch7-u6-tree-2.blurb: One question, asked of every problem: which of the five quantities is not mentioned at all?
ch7.u6.calc.c0.prompt: A scooter starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 6 s. How fast is it going at the end?
ch7.u6.calc.c0.s0: Distance is neither given nor asked for, so use v = u + at
ch7.u6.calc.c0.trap: Answering 36, which is how far it went, not how fast it is going.
ch7.u6.calc.c1.prompt: The same scooter, the same 6 seconds. How far does it travel?
ch7.u6.calc.c1.s0: The final velocity is neither given nor asked for, so use s = ut + half a t squared
ch7.u6.calc.c1.s1: The first part is zero, because u is zero
ch7.u6.calc.c1.trap: Multiplying 12 m/s by 6 s to get 72. Speed times time only works when the speed is steady, and here it climbed from zero.
ch7.u6.calc.c2.prompt: A train moving at 20 m/s brakes at 0.5 m/s² against its motion. How far does it travel before it stops?
ch7.u6.calc.c2.s0: Time is neither given nor asked for, so use 2as = v squared minus u squared
ch7.u6.calc.c2.s2: Divide minus 400 by 2 times minus 0.5, which is minus 1
ch7.u6.calc.c2.trap: Getting minus 400 and reporting it. A distance travelled is not negative: the two minus signs cancel.
ch7.u6.calc.c3.prompt: A lorry's brakes produce an acceleration of 4 m/s² against its motion, and it comes to rest 3 s later. How far does it travel while stopping?
ch7.u6.calc.c3.s0: First find how fast it was going: 0 = u minus 4 times 3, so u is 12 m/s
ch7.u6.calc.c3.s1: Now use s = ut + half a t squared
ch7.u6.calc.c3.s2: 12 times 3 is 36, and half of minus 4 times 9 is minus 18
ch7.u6.calc.c3.trap: Answering 36 by forgetting the second term. The lorry was slowing the whole time, so it covered less than a steady 12 m/s would have.
a.ch7-u6-calc-3.title: Putting them to work
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.goal: A car is doing 60 km/h on a wet road with worn tyres. From the moment the brakes bite it needs 45 m to come to rest. The lorry ahead is 28 m away. Get the braking distance down to 28 m or less.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.slower.label: Drive at 50 km/h instead of 60
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.slower.because: Braking distance goes with the square of the speed, because 2as = v² − u². Taking a sixth off the speed takes nearly a third off the distance.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.slower.wrong: Braking distance falls in step with speed, so a sixth off the speed takes a sixth off the distance.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.tyres.label: Fit new tyres
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.tyres.because: Better grip means a larger braking acceleration, and s = v² over 2a falls as a rises.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.tyres.wrong: New tyres are lighter than worn ones, and a lighter car stops sooner.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.dry.label: Wait for the road to dry
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.dry.because: A dry road grips better than a wet one, so the same brakes produce a bigger acceleration and the stop takes less road.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.dry.wrong: Rain adds weight to the car, and the extra weight is what makes it take longer.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.harder.label: Press the brake pedal harder
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.harder.because: Up to the point where the wheels lock, a harder press means a larger braking acceleration.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.harder.wrong: A harder press shortens the time, and a shorter time always means a shorter distance.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.load.label: Load the boot with sacks of rice
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.load.because: More mass with the same braking force gives a smaller acceleration, so it takes more road to stop.
chal.ch7-u6-challenge-4.load.wrong: A heavier car presses down harder and therefore grips better, so it stops sooner.
ch7.u6.challenge.debrief:
Nothing on that list is worth as much as the speed, and it is not close. Braking distance goes with the square of the velocity, so dropping from 60 to 50 does more than any set of tyres on any road surface.

It is also why drivers are told to leave a gap. Everything else on the list has to be arranged in advance. The gap is the only part of the stopping distance you get to choose while you are driving.
a.ch7-u6-challenge-4.title: Stop in time
a.ch7-u6-challenge-4.blurb: You have 28 m of clear road and you need 45 m to stop. Fix it, and say why each thing you change helps.
ch7.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: A question gives you u, a and t, and asks for s. Which equation do you reach for?
ch7.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Right. It is the one with no v in it, and v is the quantity nobody mentioned.
ch7.u6.quiz.q0.f1: There is no s anywhere in it, and an equation can only give you a quantity it contains.
ch7.u6.quiz.q0.f2: It does contain s, but it also needs v, and v is exactly what nobody gave you.
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: When are the three equations of motion valid?
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.o0: Only when the acceleration is uniform
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and that is a real restriction, not a formality.
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.f1: A bus in traffic has a changing acceleration, and all three give wrong answers for it.
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.o2: Only for objects that are falling
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.f2: Free fall is one case of uniform acceleration. It is not the only one.
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.o3: Only when the speed is constant
ch7.u6.quiz.q1.f3: At constant speed the acceleration is zero and the equations collapse to s = ut.
ch7.u6.quiz.q2.prompt: A ball is dropped and gains 10 m/s of speed in every second. How far has it fallen after 3 s?
ch7.u6.quiz.q2.f0: Right. s = 0 plus half of 10 times 9.
ch7.u6.quiz.q2.f1: That is the final speed multiplied by the time, which assumes it was doing 30 m/s all the way down.
ch7.u6.quiz.q2.f2: That is the distance after the first part of the fall, not all of it.
ch7.u6.quiz.q2.f3: That is double the right answer, which comes from forgetting the half.
a.ch7-u6-quiz-5.title: The equations
ch7.u7.circle:
Run round a rectangular track and you change direction four times a lap, once at each corner. Round a hexagon it is six times. Round an octagon, eight. Keep adding sides and the turns get smaller and come more often, and the shape creeps towards a circle.

A circle is where that line of thinking ends. The direction changes at every single point, without a pause. The speed can be perfectly steady and the velocity still never holds still for an instant, because a velocity carries a direction with it.

So a body going round a circle at a constant speed is accelerating the whole way round. That is uniform circular motion, and the moon, a satellite and a cyclist on a circular track are all doing it.

If the circle has radius r and one lap takes time t, the speed is v = 2πr / t, because 2πr is the way round.
a.ch7-u7-read-1.title: Why a circle counts as accelerating
ch7.u7.stone.predict.prompt: A small stone is tied to a thread and whirled in a circle. At the instant you let go, which way does it fly?
ch7.u7.stone.predict.o0: Straight outwards, away from the centre
ch7.u7.stone.predict.o1: Along the straight line it was already travelling at that instant
ch7.u7.stone.observe: Release at several different points of the circle and mark where the stone lands each time.
ch7.u7.stone.explain:
At every instant the stone is already moving along the tangent: the straight line that just grazes the circle at that point. The thread was the only thing bending it away from that line.

Take the thread away and nothing bends it any more, so it carries straight on in the direction it happened to be going. Release at a different point of the circle and it flies off in a different direction, which is the proof that the direction was changing all along.

A hammer thrower at a sports meet is using exactly this, and so is anyone letting go of a swing.
ch7.u7.do.steps:
1. Tie the stone firmly to one end of the thread. Tug it hard before you start.
2. Stand well clear of people, windows and animals. Everyone else stands behind the thrower.
3. Whirl the stone in a horizontal circle beside you at a steady speed.
4. Agree with a partner on a point of the circle, and let go exactly there. Chalk where it lands.
5. Repeat from three more points of the circle, marking each landing place.
6. Stand at the centre and look at your four marks. They are in four different directions.
ch7.u7.do.watch: Most students predict that the stone flies outwards along the radius. Get the prediction written down before anyone releases, or the memory quietly corrects itself afterwards.
ask.ch7-u7-do-2.whichway.q: If the stone is accelerating, which way does the acceleration point?
ask.ch7-u7-do-2.whichway.a:
Towards the centre, the whole way round.

The argument is short. The speed is not changing, so the acceleration cannot be along the direction of motion. It has to be at right angles to it, and the only direction left that keeps the stone on the circle is inwards.

You can feel it: the thread pulls on your finger, and you pull inwards on the stone. Let go and the pull stops, which is why it leaves. Class 11 gives that inward acceleration its name, and chapter 8 gives you the force behind it.
a.ch7-u7-do-2.title: Let go of the string
a.ch7-u7-do-2.blurb: Whirl a stone on a thread, release it, and watch where it actually goes. Most people guess wrong.
ch7.u7.calc.c0.prompt: An athlete runs one lap of a circular track of radius 35 m in 44 s. What is her speed? Take π as 22/7.
ch7.u7.calc.c0.s1: 2 times 22 over 7 times 35 comes to 220 m
ch7.u7.calc.c0.trap: Using the radius or the diameter as the distance. She goes round the track, not across it.
ch7.u7.calc.c1.prompt: The same lap. What is her displacement at the end of it?
ch7.u7.calc.c1.g0: She finishes at the point she started from
ch7.u7.calc.c1.s0: Displacement is the straight line from start to finish
ch7.u7.calc.c1.trap: Answering 220 m. That is how far she ran, which is a different question.
ch7.u7.calc.c2.prompt: A satellite goes once round the earth in 2 hours, on a circular path of radius 7000 km. Take π as 22/7. Find its speed in km/h.
ch7.u7.calc.c2.s1: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7000 comes to 44,000 km
ch7.u7.calc.c2.trap: Dividing by 24 out of habit. This satellite's lap takes 2 hours, not a day.
a.ch7-u7-calc-3.title: Going round
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.prompt: An object moves round a circle at a constant speed. Is it accelerating?
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.o0: No, because the speed is constant
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.f0: Constant speed is not constant velocity, and acceleration is about velocity.
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.o1: Yes, because the direction of its velocity keeps changing
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.f1: Right. The velocity is changing at every point, so there is an acceleration at every point.
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.o2: Only at the top of the circle
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.f2: No point on a circle is special. The turning is happening everywhere equally.
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.o3: Only if it is also speeding up
ch7.u7.quiz.q0.f3: Then it would not be uniform circular motion, and the question would be a different one.
ch7.u7.quiz.q1.prompt: A stone whirled on a string is released. Which way does it travel?
ch7.u7.quiz.q1.f0: Nothing is pushing it outwards. The thread was pulling it inwards, and that pull is what has just gone.
ch7.u7.quiz.q1.o1: Along the tangent at the point of release
ch7.u7.quiz.q1.f1: Right. It keeps the direction it already had at that instant.
ch7.u7.quiz.q1.f2: The inward pull is exactly the thing you have removed, so nothing is left to pull it in.
ch7.u7.quiz.q2.prompt: What distance is covered in one complete lap of a circle of radius r?
ch7.u7.quiz.q2.f0: Right, and that is the number to put on top when working out the speed.
ch7.u7.quiz.q2.f1: That is the area enclosed by the circle, not the way round it.
ch7.u7.quiz.q2.f2: That is the distance from the centre to the edge.
ch7.u7.quiz.q2.f3: That is the diameter, straight across.
a.ch7-u7-quiz-4.title: Uniform circular motion
mis.distance-equals-displacement.stateme: Distance and displacement are two names for the same thing.
mis.distance-equals-displacement.correct: They agree only when the motion is a straight line that never turns back. Turn round once and they part company.
mis.displacement-cannot-be-zero.statemen: If something has moved, its displacement cannot be zero.
mis.displacement-cannot-be-zero.correcti: A lap of a track ends where it began. The distance is the whole lap and the displacement is nothing.
mis.distance-can-be-zero.statement: Distance can come back to zero on a round trip.
mis.distance-can-be-zero.correction: Every metre covered adds to the distance and nothing takes one off again. Only displacement can return to zero.
mis.displacement-bigger-than-distance.st: Displacement can be larger than the distance covered.
mis.displacement-bigger-than-distance.co: Displacement is the straight line between the two ends, and no route between two points is shorter than that line.
mis.displacement-needs-no-direction.stat: A displacement is fully stated by its size alone.
mis.displacement-needs-no-direction.corr: 35 km leaves you standing somewhere on a circle. 35 km east is an answer.
mis.odometer-shows-displacement.statemen: An odometer shows how far a vehicle is from where it started.
mis.odometer-shows-displacement.correcti: It counts wheel turns, so it adds up every metre driven, the way back included.
mis.motion-is-absolute.statement: An object is either moving or it is not, and there is nothing more to say.
mis.motion-is-absolute.correction: It is moving compared to something. Name the reference point first, or the statement means nothing.
mis.uniform-means-fast.correction: It means equal distances in equal times, at any speed at all. A tortoise manages it easily.
mis.average-speed-is-mean-of-speeds.stat: Average speed is the average of the speeds.
mis.average-speed-is-mean-of-speeds.corr: It is the total distance over the total time. Averaging the speeds is right only when equal times are spent at each.
mis.average-velocity-uses-distance.state: Average velocity is the total distance divided by the total time.
mis.average-velocity-uses-distance.corre: That is average speed. Average velocity uses the displacement, which is often a much smaller number.
mis.average-velocity-shortcut-always.sta: Average velocity is always halfway between the starting and finishing velocities.
mis.average-velocity-shortcut-always.cor: Only while the velocity is changing at a steady rate. Otherwise it is displacement over time and nothing else.
mis.speed-is-velocity.statement: Speed and velocity are the same quantity.
mis.speed-is-velocity.correction: Speed is a size. Velocity is a size with a direction, which is why it changes on a bend while the speed does not.
mis.velocity-needs-speed-change.statemen: A velocity can only change if the speed changes.
mis.velocity-needs-speed-change.correcti: A change of direction changes the velocity on its own. That is the whole of uniform circular motion.
mis.negative-acceleration-means-backward: A negative acceleration means the object is moving backwards.
It means the acceleration points against the motion. A car braking while going forwards has one.
mis.acceleration-means-speeding-up.corre: It means the velocity is changing. Slowing down is acceleration too, with the opposite sign.
mis.no-velocity-no-acceleration.statemen: If the velocity is zero at some instant, the acceleration must be zero too.
mis.no-velocity-no-acceleration.correcti: A ball at the top of its throw is momentarily still and is still being accelerated downwards.
mis.acceleration-is-time-over-velocity.s: Acceleration is the time divided by the change in velocity.
mis.acceleration-is-time-over-velocity.c: It is the other way up: the change in velocity divided by the time it took to happen.
mis.uniform-acceleration-means-uniform-v: Uniform acceleration and uniform velocity are the same thing.
Uniform velocity means it is not changing at all. Uniform acceleration means it is changing at a steady rate.
mis.flat-line-always-means-stopped.state: A flat line on any motion graph means the object has stopped.
mis.flat-line-always-means-stopped.corre: On a distance-time graph, yes. On a velocity-time graph a flat line above zero means a steady speed.
mis.steeper-means-further.statement: The steeper line on a distance-time graph has gone further.
mis.steeper-means-further.correction: Steeper means faster. How far each has gone is read off the height at the time you care about.
mis.area-under-distance-graph.statement: The area under a distance-time graph gives the distance.
mis.area-under-distance-graph.correction: Area means something only under a velocity-time graph. Under a distance-time graph it means nothing at all.
The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the distance.
Slope gives the acceleration. The distance is the area underneath the line.
mis.graph-is-the-route.statement: A distance-time graph is a picture of the route the object took.
mis.graph-is-the-route.correction: It is a graph, not a map. A car on a winding road can still draw a perfectly straight line on it.
mis.equations-work-everywhere.statement: The three equations of motion work for any motion at all.
mis.equations-work-everywhere.correction: Only for uniform acceleration. A bus in city traffic breaks every one of them.
Distance is always the speed multiplied by the time.
Only while the speed is steady. When it is changing, use the average velocity or the equation with the half in it.
mis.slower-speed-same-fraction-of-distan: Halving the speed halves the braking distance.
Braking distance goes with the square of the speed, so halving the speed quarters it.
mis.heavier-stops-sooner.statement: A heavier vehicle stops in a shorter distance because it grips the road harder.
mis.heavier-stops-sooner.correction: More mass with the same braking force gives a smaller acceleration, so it takes more road to stop.
mis.circular-motion-not-accelerated.stat: Going round a circle at a steady speed is not acceleration.
mis.circular-motion-not-accelerated.corr: The direction changes at every point, so the velocity never holds still. That is acceleration.
mis.released-stone-flies-outward.stateme: Release a whirling stone and it flies straight outwards from the centre.
mis.released-stone-flies-outward.correct: It leaves along the tangent, in the direction it was already travelling at that instant.
mis.circumference-is-pi-r-squared.statem: The way round a circle of radius r is πr².
mis.circumference-is-pi-r-squared.correc: That is the area enclosed. The way round is 2πr.
mis.lap-displacement-is-half.statement: After one complete lap, the displacement is half the length of the track.
mis.lap-displacement-is-half.correction: Half a lap would leave the runner across the track. A full lap brings her back to the start, so the displacement is nothing.
mis.displacement-needs-distance.statemen: A displacement means nothing unless the distance covered is quoted beside it.
mis.displacement-needs-distance.correcti: They answer two different questions and each one stands alone. 35 km east is a complete displacement.
mis.uniform-is-accelerated.statement: Covering equal distances in equal times is accelerated motion.
mis.uniform-is-accelerated.correction: It is the opposite. Accelerated motion covers unequal distances in equal times.
mis.uniform-means-circular.statement: Uniform motion means going round and round.
mis.uniform-means-circular.correction: Uniform is about equal distances in equal times. The path can be dead straight.
mis.distance-read-as-speed.statement: A distance given in the question can be the answer to a question about speed.
mis.distance-read-as-speed.correction: A speed is always a distance divided by a time. Reading a number straight off the question skips the division.
mis.average-is-one-stretch.statement: The average speed is the speed over one stretch of the journey.
mis.average-is-one-stretch.correction: It is the total distance over the total time. One stretch is only part of each of those.
mis.odometer-confused-with-other-dials.s: The odometer is the dial that shows the speed, or how long the vehicle has been running.
mis.odometer-confused-with-other-dials.c: It counts wheel turns, so it shows distance. The speedometer shows speed and a clock shows time.
mis.speed-settles-velocity-questions.sta: Whether speed and velocity agree depends on how fast the object is going.
mis.speed-settles-velocity-questions.cor: It depends on the shape of the path. A slow walk round a block has them disagreeing just as much as a fast one.
mis.velocity-keeps-its-first-direction.s: The average velocity of a lap points the way the object set off.
mis.velocity-keeps-its-first-direction.c: Average velocity comes from the displacement, and the displacement for a lap has no length and so no direction.
mis.lap-velocity-unknowable.statement: The average velocity for a complete lap cannot be worked out.
mis.lap-velocity-unknowable.correction: It can, and it is zero. A lap hands you both ends of the journey and they are the same point.
mis.steady-speed-means-steady-position.s: If the speed is not changing, the distance from the start is not changing either.
mis.steady-speed-means-steady-position.c: A steady speed means the distance grows steadily. It stops growing only when the speed is zero.
mis.acceleration-needs-speed-change.stat: There can be no acceleration unless the speed changes.
mis.acceleration-needs-speed-change.corr: A change of direction is a change of velocity, and that is an acceleration whatever the speed does.
A negative acceleration means the object has already come to rest.
It means the object is slowing. It stops only when the velocity itself reaches zero.
mis.thrown-ball-keeps-an-upward-push.sta: A ball thrown upwards carries an upward push with it while it rises.
mis.thrown-ball-keeps-an-upward-push.cor: Nothing pushes it once it has left the hand. It rises because it was given speed, and gravity pulls it down the whole time.
mis.area-confused-with-the-axes.statemen: The area under a velocity-time graph gives one of the quantities on its axes.
mis.area-confused-with-the-axes.correcti: Each axis gives one number on its own: a height is a velocity, a width is a time. The area is the two multiplied, which is a distance.
mis.steeper-means-started-earlier.statem: A steeper line on a distance-time graph means that object set off earlier.
mis.steeper-means-started-earlier.correc: Where a line meets the axis says when it set off. How steep it is says how fast it is going.
mis.any-slope-means-accelerating.stateme: A sloping line on a distance-time graph means the object is accelerating.
mis.any-slope-means-accelerating.correct: A straight slope means a steady speed. Acceleration shows up as a curve.
mis.first-equation-for-distance.statemen: v = u + at can be used to find a distance.
mis.first-equation-for-distance.correcti: There is no s anywhere in it, and an equation can only give you a quantity it contains.
mis.any-equation-with-s-will-do.statemen: Any equation containing s can be used to find s.
mis.any-equation-with-s-will-do.correcti: It must also contain only quantities you have. 2as = v² − u² needs v, and v is the one nobody mentioned.
mis.equations-only-for-falling.statement: The equations of motion apply only to falling bodies.
mis.equations-only-for-falling.correctio: Free fall is one case of uniform acceleration. A train pulling away from a platform is another.
mis.equations-need-constant-speed.statem: The equations of motion need the speed to be constant.
mis.equations-need-constant-speed.correc: At constant speed the acceleration is zero and they collapse to s = ut. They are built for a velocity that is changing steadily.
mis.t-not-squared.statement: In s = ut + ½at² the time is used once rather than squared.
mis.t-not-squared.correction: The t is squared. Leaving it as t gives 15 m instead of 45 m for a fall of three seconds.
mis.half-left-out.statement: The half in s = ut + ½at² can be dropped.
mis.half-left-out.correction: Without it the answer doubles. The half is there because the object spent the whole time speeding up, rather than travelling at its final speed.
mis.circle-turns-only-at-points.statemen: On a circular path the turning happens at particular points rather than everywhere.
mis.circle-turns-only-at-points.correcti: A circle has no corners. The direction is changing at every point, equally.
mis.released-stone-flies-inward.statemen: Release a whirling stone and it moves in towards the centre.
mis.released-stone-flies-inward.correcti: The inward pull is the thing you have just removed. Nothing is left to pull it in.
mis.lap-is-a-straight-measure.statement: The distance round a circle is one of its straight measurements, the radius or the diameter.
mis.lap-is-a-straight-measure.correction: Those are straight lines drawn through the circle. The way round is 2πr, more than three times the diameter.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track. Give her distance and her displacement.
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: The distance is 400 m, the whole way round. The displacement is zero, because she finishes at the point she started from.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 400 m given twice. The two are being answered as one question out of habit, and a lap is the case where they differ most.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: Why does saying that the school is 2 km away not actually locate the school?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: Because it never says 2 km from where. A position needs a reference point before the number means anything, and the reference point is a choice somebody has to make and state.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because it does not give the direction'. True, and only half of it. The missing reference point is the bigger gap.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Name the two things that have to be equal before a motion can be called uniform.
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: Equal distances, in equal intervals of time. Both together, and nothing about the speed being high or low.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'it has to be fast'. Speed does not appear in the definition at all, and a tortoise can manage uniform motion.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: A bus covers 60 km in the first hour and 40 km in the next two hours. Tell me its average speed, and say why it is not 50 km/h.
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: 100 km over 3 hours, which is about 33 km/h. Averaging 60 and 40 would be right only if equal time had been spent on each stretch, and twice as long was spent on the slower one.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for 50 km/h. It is the answer that comes from averaging the two speeds, and it is the single most common slip in this topic.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Describe a journey in which the average speed is large and the average velocity is zero.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Any journey that ends where it began. A swimmer doing lengths of a pool, a runner finishing a lap, a bus on a round trip. The distance piles up while the displacement comes back to nothing.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for an answer that changes the speed rather than the path. Speed is not the lever here: finishing at the starting point is.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: When do the average speed and the magnitude of the average velocity come to the same number?
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: When the motion is along a straight line and never turns back. Then the route and the straight line between the ends are the same thing.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'when the object is moving fast'. Speed has nothing to do with whether the two agree.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: A car is moving forwards and its acceleration is minus 3 m/s². Describe what the car is doing.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Moving forwards and slowing down. The minus sign says the acceleration points against the motion, not that the car has turned round.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'it is reversing'. The sign belongs to the acceleration, and the direction of travel is a separate question.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: A ball thrown straight up is momentarily still at the top of its flight. Is its acceleration zero at that instant?
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: No. It is still about 10 m/s² downwards, which is exactly why the ball does not hang there and instead starts to come back down.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'yes, because it is not moving'. Velocity and acceleration are separate quantities, and one being zero says nothing about the other.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: Name the four things you can read off a distance-time graph and a velocity-time graph.
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: On the distance-time graph: the height is where the object is, and the slope is how fast it is going. On the velocity-time graph: the height is how fast it is going, and the slope is the acceleration. The area under the velocity-time graph is the distance.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for the area being claimed for the distance-time graph. Area means nothing there, and the habit of looking for it comes straight from the other graph.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: A flat line turns up on a distance-time graph, and then on a velocity-time graph. Tell me what each one means.
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Flat on a distance-time graph means the object is not moving. Flat on a velocity-time graph, above zero, means it is moving at a steady speed. Only a flat line along zero on the velocity-time graph means stopped.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'stopped' given twice. The shape is identical and the meaning is not, and this is the commonest graph error in the chapter.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: A problem gives you u, a and t, and asks for s. Name the equation you would use, and say how you knew.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: s = ut + ½at². The quantity nobody mentioned is v, and that is the only equation of the three with no v in it.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for the right equation with no reason behind it. Remembering which is which is guesswork; spotting the missing quantity works every time.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: When are the three equations of motion not allowed?
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: Whenever the acceleration is not uniform. They are built on the velocity changing at a steady rate, and a bus in traffic breaks all three.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'when the object is not going in a straight line'. True as far as it goes, but the restriction that catches people in an exam is uniform acceleration.
recap.s.u7.q1.ask: A cyclist rides round a circular track at a steady 15 km/h. Is she accelerating? Explain the answer.
recap.s.u7.q1.answer: Yes, the whole way round. Her speed never changes but her direction does, at every point, and a velocity is a speed with a direction. A changing velocity is an acceleration.
recap.s.u7.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'no, the speed is constant'. Constant speed is not constant velocity, and that one distinction is the entire topic.
recap.s.u7.q2.ask: You let go of a whirling stone. Describe the path it takes from that instant onwards.
recap.s.u7.q2.answer: It travels along the tangent: the straight line it was already moving along at the moment of release. Release at a different point of the circle and it leaves in a different direction.
recap.s.u7.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'straight outwards from the centre'. Most of a class predicts that, which is why the prediction is worth writing down before anyone lets go.
aid.s.u1.meaning: A span is the straight reach from one end of a thing to the other, which is exactly what a displacement is. The distance is how you got there.
aid.s.u1.S.property: Size: which of the two is never the smaller?
aid.s.u1.S.a: Never smaller. It is at least as big as the displacement, and usually bigger.
aid.s.u1.S.b: Never bigger than the distance. At most equal to it.
aid.s.u1.P.property: Path: how much of the route is counted?
aid.s.u1.P.a: All of it. Every step, in whatever direction it was taken.
aid.s.u1.P.b: None of it. Only the straight line from the first point to the last.
aid.s.u1.A.property: Arrow: does the answer need a direction?
aid.s.u1.A.a: No. 85 km is a complete answer on its own.
aid.s.u1.A.b: Yes. 35 km is not an answer until you say 35 km east.
aid.s.u1.N.property: Nil: can it come out as zero after a journey?
aid.s.u1.N.a: No. Once you have moved, it can only grow.
aid.s.u1.N.b: Yes, on any round trip. Back where you started means a displacement of nothing.
tree.equation.root.label: A problem with uniform acceleration
tree.equation.root.q: Of the five quantities u, v, a, t and s, which one does the problem neither give you nor ask for?
tree.equation.first.label: v = u + at
tree.equation.second.label: s = ut + ½at²
tree.equation.third.label: 2as = v² − u²
gloss.motion: A change of position with time, always measured against some other thing that is taken to be fixed.
gloss.reference-point: The fixed thing a position is measured from. Also called the origin. Any convenient thing will do, but one has to be chosen and stated.
gloss.distance: The total length of the route actually covered, whatever direction each part of it was in. It has a size and no direction.
gloss.displacement: The straight line from the starting point to the finishing point, with its direction. It can be zero even after a long journey.
gloss.magnitude: The numerical size of a quantity, with its direction left out. The magnitude of a velocity is the speed.
gloss.uniform-motion: Motion in which equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time, however small those intervals are. Nothing about it says fast or slow.
gloss.non-uniform-motion: Motion in which unequal distances are covered in equal intervals of time. A vehicle on a crowded road is the standard example.
gloss.speed: Distance covered per unit time. Its SI unit is the metre per second. It has a size and no direction.
gloss.average-speed: The total distance divided by the total time. It is not the average of the separate speeds unless equal times were spent at each.
gloss.velocity: The speed of an object together with its direction. It changes if the speed changes, if the direction changes, or if both do.
gloss.average-velocity: The displacement divided by the time taken. When the velocity changes at a steady rate it is also the mean of the starting and finishing velocities.
gloss.acceleration: The change in velocity per unit time. Its SI unit is the metre per second squared. It is negative when it points against the motion.
gloss.uniform-acceleration: Acceleration that does not change: the velocity rises or falls by equal amounts in equal intervals of time. A freely falling body is the usual example.
gloss.distance-time-graph: A graph of distance against time. Its height tells you where the object is and its slope tells you how fast. Area under it means nothing.
gloss.velocity-time-graph: A graph of velocity against time. Its height is the velocity, its slope is the acceleration, and the area under it is the distance covered.
gloss.slope: How steeply a line on a graph rises: the change up the side divided by the change along the bottom. What it stands for depends on what the two axes are.
gloss.equations-of-motion: The three relations between u, v, a, t and s that hold while the acceleration is uniform. Each one leaves out exactly one of the five quantities.
gloss.uniform-circular-motion: Motion round a circular path at a constant speed. The direction of the velocity changes at every point, so it is accelerated motion throughout.
gloss.tangent: The straight line that just grazes a circle at one point. A body released from a circular path leaves along it.
gloss.circumference: The distance once round a circle, equal to 2 times pi times the radius. Not to be confused with the area, which is pi times the radius squared.
gloss.odometer: The instrument in a vehicle that counts the distance it has travelled, by counting wheel turns. It knows nothing about displacement.
